stories.title: Novo modelo da OpenAI identifica centenas de falhas de segurança
stories.summary: A OpenAI restringirá o acesso ao modelo a equipes aprovadas no Daybreak, programa que inclui defesa e testes de segurança O post Novo modelo da OpenAI identifica centenas de falhas de segurança apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

sources.name: Olhar Digital IA
sources.title: Novo modelo da OpenAI identifica centenas de falhas de segurança
sources.text: A OpenAI apresentou o GPT-6 Cyber, modelo de inteligência artificial especializado em cibersegurança que já identificou e validou milhares de explorações em softwares como Linux e Firefox. A ferramenta também desenvolve métodos para explorar vulnerabilidades e ajuda a propor correções. O acesso será restrito a profissionais e organizações aprovados pela empresa, por meio do programa de segurança Daybreak. O GPT-6 Cyber alcançou 48,5% de aproveitamento no ExploitGym, avaliação que mede a capacidade de explorar vulnerabilidades específicas em sistemas remotos. O resultado representa uma melhora relativa de 51% em relação ao GPT-5.6 Cyber, que obteve 32,1%. Em outro teste, voltado à identificação de falhas em aplicações web sem acesso ao código-fonte, o novo modelo identificou 40,3% das vulnerabilidades , contra 32% do GPT-6 Astra . A OpenAI também avaliou se a ferramenta respeita os limites definidos pelos pesquisadores. Sem instruções adicionais de segurança, o GPT-6 Cyber evitou explorar serviços fora do escopo autorizado em 99,93% dos testes. Com as instruções de implantação, o índice chegou a 100%. A empresa classificou o modelo como Crítico em cibersegurança , uma categoria acima da classificação Alta atribuída ao GPT-5.6 Cyber em sua estrutura de avaliação de riscos. Os resultados também aparecem em pesquisas com projetos de código aberto. No Linux , o GPT-6 Cyber reproduziu 1.724 vulnerabilidades e desenvolveu explorações funcionais para 948 delas. O número é mais de cinco vezes superior aos 166 casos explorados pelo GPT-5.6 Sol com o mesmo método de pesquisa. A OpenAI informou que comunicou 304 descobertas críticas aos responsáveis pelo projeto, acompanhadas de possíveis correções. As demais vulnerabilidades também estão em processo de correção. No Firefox , o modelo identificou 81 vulnerabilidades inéditas classificadas como de alta gravidade pela Mozilla. O trabalho também mostrou que outros 30 problemas já conhecidos eram mais graves do que se acreditava anteriormente. A OpenAI forneceu testes reproduzíveis e propostas de correção à equipe do navegador, que começou a disponibilizar atualizações para resolver parte das falhas encontradas. O GPT-6 Cyber integra o Daybreak, programa da OpenAI voltado à pesquisa e à defesa em segurança digital. A iniciativa possui três modalidades: Inicialmente, o GPT-6 Cyber estará disponível pela API e pelo Codex para um grupo selecionado de clientes aprovados do Daybreak Red. A OpenAI pretende ampliar gradualmente o acesso aos demais participantes dessa modalidade. A empresa também anunciou um programa de subsídios de US$ 1 bilhão para facilitar o acesso às ferramentas do Daybreak por equipes com recursos limitados, incluindo órgãos governamentais e prestadores de serviços essenciais. Para reduzir o risco de uso indevido, a OpenAI implementou monitoramento de atividades suspeitas, restrições ao uso de credenciais comprometidas e mecanismos para bloquear assistência em ataques não autorizados contra sistemas críticos. A empresa também recomenda ambientes isolados e supervisão humana em operações de alto risco. Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo. Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

sources.name: Tecmundo
sources.title: OpenAI lança GPT-6 Cyber e afirma que modelo caça falhas sem desobedecer pesquisadores
sources.text: A OpenAI apresentou, nesta quinta-feira (5), o GPT-6 Cyber , um modelo de inteligência artificial (IA) voltado para a segurança digital que supera versões anteriores na identificação de vulnerabilidades em sistemas de computadores . A ferramenta foi classificada como “crítica” para a segurança cibernética devido ao alto potencial técnico. Segundo a big tech, o modelo alcançou, em testes práticos realizados em ambientes controlados, um índice de acerto de quase 50% na exploração de falhas remotas, o que superou os 32,1% registrados pelo antecessor (o GPT-5.6 Cyber ). A tecnologia também apresentou maior precisão para respeitar as regras estabelecidas pelos pesquisadores. O GPT‐6 Cyber é um grande salto na pesquisa de segurança: mais capaz de encontrar e corrigir vulnerabilidades e permanecer muito mais confiável dentro dos limites estabelecidos pelos pesquisadores. “Essa melhoria no alinhamento reflete o treinamento dedicado para permanecer dentro do escopo autorizado, respeitar as restrições e relatar os resultados com precisão”, completou a OpenAI , em comunicado oficial . Durante os testes de validação, os analistas aplicaram o sistema no código do kernel Linux . O modelo reproduziu milhares de falhas conhecidas e gerou códigos de exploração funcionais para centenas delas. A partir dessa ação, a empresa relatou que centenas de problemas críticos foram enviados aos mantenedores do software acompanhados de propostas de correção. Paralelamente, o sistema atuou no navegador Firefox , no qual documentou dezenas de falhas inéditas classificadas como “de alta gravidade”. A Mozilla , a organização responsável pelo desenvolvimento do navegador, iniciou a liberação de atualizações de segurança para corrigir os problemas identificados pela IA. Para evitar usos indevidos, a OpenAI explicou ter implementado salvaguardas que monitoram as ações do modelo e bloqueiam tentativas de comprometer controles industriais e infraestruturas essenciais. O desenvolvimento dessas proteções contou com a colaboração da empresa de segurança cibernética Dragos, que testou os modelos em laboratório e publicou os resultados em uma análise técnica . O piso de habilidade está caindo para o reconhecimento e a pesquisa de vulnerabilidade necessária antes de um ataque A companhia frisou que o acesso ao novo modelo está restrito a clientes selecionados e aprovados que participam do programa voltado para testes autorizados e pesquisas avançadas de segurança Siga o TecMundo no X , Instagram , Facebook e YouTube e assine a nossa newsletter para receber as principais notícias e análises diretamente no seu e-mail. stories.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
stories.summary: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion as part of a funding round that hasn't closed yet but is expected to in the coming weeks.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
sources.text: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion. Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg. In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target. TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds. The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago. OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point. The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future. sources.name: SiliconANGLE
sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises $11B in new funding at $1.25T valuation
sources.text: OpenAI Group PBC has reportedly raised $11 billion as part of a funding round that could nearly double in size over the coming weeks, as s ources told Bloomberg that investors wired the funds to the company today. The tipsters didn’t name the backers. The list of possible participants includes Microsoft Corp., which contributed to at least four of OpenAI’s previous rounds. That included its most recent $122 billion raise in March, which also drew the participation of Nvidia Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and about two dozen others. It’s believed that OpenAI could raise up to $9 billion in additional funding as part of the round. The deal is expected to value the company at $1.25 billion. That potentially puts it on track to surpass Anthropic PBC’s market capitalization. Anthropic hopes to achieve a valuation of $1.5 trillion in its upcoming initial public offering. However, several of its investors reportedly don’t consider that to be a realistic goal. According to the Wall Street Journal , one shareholder reportedly suggested that the company pursue a valuation closer to $1 trillion. Anthropic’s IPO filing revealed that its quarterly revenue jumped 1,127% on a year-over-year basis in the third quarter. Last month, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI closed the quarter with $50 billion in net annualized revenue, which represented a 77% year-over-year increase. The company’s growth was driven by its enterprise business, which saw sales more than double. The latest addition to OpenAI’s enterprise portfolio debuted on Thursday. GPT-6 Cyber can perform most cybersecurity tasks better than GPT-6 Astra, the company’s most capable general-purpose model. OpenAI engineers used it to develop 948 Linux⁠ exploits and uncover 81 high-severity zero-day flaws in Firefox. OpenAI President Greg Brockman revealed on Wednesday that the company had experienced a slowdown in the first half of the year. Its growth started accelerating after the June launch of GPT-5.6 Sol, the immediate predecessor to GPT-6 Astra. Brockman added that OpenAI’s ChatGPT Work productivity application and coding tools played a role as well. The company plans to go public sometime in 2027. Today’s cash infusion should make it easier for OpenAI to finance its steep infrastructure expenses until the listing. In July, The Information reported that the ChatGPT developer has more than $665 billion worth of chip and data center commitments. OpenAI has developed a custom inference accelerator in collaboration with Broadcom Inc. as part of an effort to lower its long-term hardware spending. Anthropic, for its part, is expected to kick off its IPO roadmap next week. The company reportedly plans to go public before Thanksgiving. stories.title: Nine engineers, 1,211 code updates in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork
stories.summary: The post Nine engineers, 1,211 code updates in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork appeared first on Source .

sources.name: Microsoft Source
sources.title: Nine engineers, 1,211 code updates in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork
sources.text: Plus a case study where we put everything together by moving our runtime from Python to Rust while live. In January of this year, a small team at Microsoft set out to build Copilot Cowork , an agentic execution layer that performs multi-step workflows on a user’s behalf. That result brings the powerful AI-assisted tools and capabilities developers have today to everyday knowledge workers, all with Work IQ , Microsoft 365 security and governance, cloud execution, and Microsoft’s multi-model architecture. This is the story of how the team took Copilot Cowork from an empty repo to worldwide GA in about four and a half months, then moved its runtime from Python to Rust while it was live. Agents wrote most of the code. Ways of working changed along the way, and the practices other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team: moving fast while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. On October 21, nine engineers merged 1,211 pull requests into the main branch of the Copilot Cowork backend. That number would have sounded absurd to the team in January, when a handful of us made the first commit to an empty repo. Agents wrote most of the code, but engineers remained responsible for defining the work and judging the results. Our small team wrote clearer specs, set architecture and security boundaries, and focused its review on higher-risk changes, production impact, and cases where checks or reviewers disagreed. Automated checks and agent reviewers examined every change. Agents could propose changes, but they could not decide what was allowed to happen. We didn’t plan on working this way. But every few weeks, the agents got better, part of our process stopped working, and we adapted. Six practices emerged from those changes. They cover how we specify work, run agents within clear boundaries, test our checks, preserve what the team learns, shape the codebase for parallel work, and set limits on automated loops. They aren’t a recipe for matching our PR count. They are lessons other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. We’ll end with the project that puts those practices to the test together: moving the live runtime from Python to Rust. The first commit was made on January 13. From the start, agents wrote the code. In the first weeks, we learned that the agent was rarely what slowed us down. The bottleneck was not knowing exactly what we wanted. A vague request got us code that looked reasonable, survived a quick read, and then did the wrong thing. Fixing it took longer than writing a proper request would have in the first place. So we adopted a rule that still stands today: no code without a markdown spec written first. The spec covers three things: A good spec saves far more time than it costs upfront. But a weak one leads to rework a few days later. The faster agents became at implementation, the more important it became for us to be precise about intent, requirements, and what good looked like. Many of our specs start out spoken. Someone talks through a feature, and an agent turns that into a first draft of the spec, which the human then edits. I think this did more for our speed than any single model upgrade. We launched Copilot Cowork to our first enterprise customers in the Frontier program on March 30. The next step was running more than one agent at a time. Each works in its own copy of the repo, on one task, from one spec. One agent became five, and five became dozens. Merged PRs per month went from 257 in January to 2,754 in May. Our busiest week before GA had 783. Parallel work went better than we expected for two reasons: In Copilot Cowork, the model runs in a container without user credentials. A trusted host outside the container handles identity, policy, approvals, and tools, and every Microsoft 365 operation goes through the host. We didn’t want to limit what the agent could attempt, because a heavily restricted agent isn’t very useful . With our architecture, the model can plan and ask for anything, and the host decides what actually happens. That separation lets us increase the number of agents working in parallel without giving the model credentials or direct authority over operations. The host still applied identity, policy, approvals, and audit at the point of execution. Building that in at the start was much easier than adding it later would’ve been. It also helped in a way we didn’t plan for. The agent only talks to the host through a defined interface, so we could later replace the entire host without changing the agent—which we did when we migrated to Rust. We reached worldwide general availability on June 16, about four and a half months after the first commit, with several models and 16 plugins. With agents writing most of the code, nine people couldn’t read every change, and waiting for a human review was becoming the slowest step for every PR. Several engineers each built their own review bot, modeled on how they review code themselves, and the bots competed. When one bot caught a problem another had missed, the bot that missed it got a new rule. Over time, each reviewer built up a large set of rules learned from its own misses. Each one has now been through at least10,000 generations; in each generation, the reviewer runs reviews, then reflects on what it missed and gets better at reviewing code. Today, a useful first review usually arrives within several minutes of a pull request being opened. On a sample of recent merged PRs, the median was about four and a half minutes. The author gets quick feedback while the change is still fresh, and the detailed reading still happens. Of course, reviewer agents can still miss things. Once, a group of reviewer agents read a change in one of the most sensitive parts of the product. Each had been told to try to break it, and none found a problem.
